title: Ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityaḥ: the Sun as all things
theme: A prayer to be repeated by one who cannot perform the meditations taught before it: the Sun moves untiring, the rivers flow with what he gives, and all that is — the waters, light, the deathless, the Veda, the worlds and Om — is he.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «दीप्तिमत्त्वाद्घृणिः» — ghṛṇi because he shines
The anonymous commentator: «जगत्प्रसवहेतुत्वात्सूर्यः» — sūrya because he brings the world forth

words.meaning: like (here a particle of comparison, not of negation)
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «नकार उपमार्थः» — na means ‘like’
The anonymous commentator: he moves by the path of the sky, day after day, to serve the worlds
The anonymous commentator: «क्षरणराहित्येन नित्यत्वादक्षरमक्षरः» — imperishable because it does not wane

words.role: main verb; the rivers are supplied as subject
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «क्षरन्ति नद्यो वहन्ति» — the rivers carry it
The anonymous commentator: «तस्मात्पूर्वोक्तादादित्याज्जन्यं रसमुदकं» — the water born of the sun
The anonymous commentator: «तदादित्यलक्षणं ब्रह्म» — that brahman marked by the sun

words.role: one of the list of what ‘that’ is

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «ब्रह्म त्रयोविद्या» — here the threefold Veda

sandhi.rule: ghṛṇiḥ + sūryaḥ: the visarga becomes s before s (P. 8.3.36 (वा शरि)); the Taittirīya recitation writes the doubled sibilant स्स.

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: -aḥ loses its visarga before a vowel other than a, and the vowels stay apart (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
-aḥ becomes -o before a voiced sound (P. 6.1.114 (हशि च)).

sandhi.type: final t before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: t becomes d before a voiced consonant (P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते)).
jyotiḥ (= jyotir) + rasaḥ: the first r drops and the vowel before it is lengthened (P. 8.3.14 (रो रि), P. 6.3.111 (ढ्रलोपे पूर्वस्य दीर्घोऽणः)).

sandhi.type: visarga before s; r before a vowel
sandhi.rule: bhuvaḥ + suvaḥ → bhuvas suvaḥ (spelled स्स); suvar + om → suvar om, the r of suvar showing before the vowel.

morphology.note: Neuter in form, describing the sun; the anonymous commentator restores the masculine («अक्षरमक्षरः»).
In the Veda na after a noun can mean ‘like’; the commentator takes it so here («नकार उपमार्थः»), so the line compares the sun’s course to the course of light.
In the third line it stands in a list of nominatives; it is read as a nominative (‘that essence’), as the commentator’s gloss «रसं मधुरादिरसज्ञातम्» treats it.

translation.literal: The blazing one, Sūrya, Āditya, like light moves, imperishable. They [the rivers] pour honey, that essence. That truly [is] the real: the essence, the waters, light, sap, the deathless, brahman, bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ, Om.
translation.readable: The blazing Sun, son of Aditi, travels like light itself, never failing. The rivers pour out sweetness, the water that comes from him. And that is the real: the essence of things, the waters, light, the sap of life, the deathless, the Veda, the three worlds and Om — all of it is the Sun.

anvaya: घृणिः सूर्यः आदित्यः प्रभा न अक्षरम् वाति । [सिन्धवः] तत् रसम् मधु क्षरन्ति । तत् वै सत्यम् — रसम् आपः ज्योतिः रसः अमृतम् ब्रह्म भूः भुवः सुवः ओम् ।
syntax: Three statements. The first: three names of the sun as subject, a comparison (prabhā na) and a verb of motion (vāti) with the predicate akṣaram. The second: a verb in the plural whose subject, the rivers, is supplied by the commentator, with madhu and tad rasam as objects. The third: a nominal sentence identifying ‘that’ with the true, followed by a list of nominatives without a verb, ending in the three vyāhṛtis and Om.

ambiguities.note: Negation (‘light does not move’) or comparison (‘like light’). The anonymous commentator takes the comparison and says it is an impossible simile: the sun has nothing to be compared with but his own light.

The verb is plural with no subject. The anonymous commentator supplies the rivers, which carry the water the sun’s rain gives («आदित्यलब्धवृष्ट्युदकमेव नद्यो वहन्ति»); Sāyaṇa, on his own text of the mantra, supplies the worshippers, who offer sweet things to the sun.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A japa formula in prose (yajus). Bhāskara calls its first part an eight-syllable mantra of the sun ending in Om («सावित्रोऽष्टाक्षरः प्रणवान्तो मन्त्रः»): ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityaḥ om.

beginner: This short prayer is for someone who cannot manage the longer meditations the text has just taught. They are told simply to repeat it. It names the Sun three times — the blazing one, the one who brings the world forth, the son of Aditi — and says he travels through the sky like light itself and never fails. The rivers, it says, flow with sweet water, because their water comes from the rain the Sun brings. The last line is a list: the true, the essence of things, the waters, light, the sap of life, the deathless, the Veda, earth, mid-air, heaven, and the sound Om. The old commentator explains the point: the one who repeats it should hold in mind that all of these are the Sun. Two other commentators knew the prayer in a different wording.
analogy: Like a child told that bread comes from the farmer, the rain, the field and the sun at once, and learning to see the sun in every slice.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It names the sun three times and says he moves like light, imperishable; that sweetness flows, ‘that essence’; and that ‘that’ is the real — the essence, the waters, light, sap, the deathless, brahman, the three worlds and Om.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator introduces it as a prayer to be repeated, addressed to the Sun, for one unable to perform the meditations taught before: «पूर्वोक्तोपासनास्वसमर्थस्याऽऽदित्यदेवताविषयं जप्यं मन्त्रमाह». Sāyaṇa, on the same mantra in his own recension, says the same: «उपासनायामसमर्थस्याऽऽदित्यदेवताविषयं जप्यं मन्त्रमाह».

commentary.q: How does the commentator read the second half?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: As a statement that the Sun, as brahman, is everything: «उत्तरार्धेनाऽऽदित्यब्रह्मणः सर्वात्मकत्वमुच्यते». Each item of the list is glossed — brahman as the threefold Veda («ब्रह्म त्रयोविद्या»), bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ as the three worlds — and the one who repeats the mantra is to hold in mind that all of it is the Sun: «एतत्सर्वमादित्य एवेति मनसा विभावयेदिति भावः».

commentary.q: How do Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara read it?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Both comment on a different wording of the mantra. Their text continues after ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityaḥ with ‘they worship’, ‘austerity, truth’, and ‘that is brahman, that is the waters’, where this text has ‘like light moves, imperishable’ and ‘that essence’. Sāyaṇa glosses Āditya as the son of the goddess Aditi («आदित्योऽदितिदेवतायाः पुत्रः»). Bhāskara calls the first part an eight-syllable mantra of the Sun ending in Om, famous in the Kāṭhaka («सावित्रोऽष्टाक्षरः प्रणवान्तो मन्त्रः काठके विख्यातवैभवः»), whose subject is the supreme brahman favouring the world in the form of the Sun («सवितृरूपेण जगदनुगृह्णानं परं ब्रह्मास्य प्रतिपाद्यम्»).

commentary.q: What is the comparison in ‘na prabhā’?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The commentator takes na as a particle of comparison («नकार उपमार्थः»): the sun moves like light. He adds that the comparison is in fact impossible, since the sun has no likeness but his own light.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. The anonymous commentator, Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara read the mantra as a prayer to the Sun identified with brahman; none of them argues it as a doctrine of one school against another. Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

parallels.note: The Chāndogya calls the sun the honey of the gods and builds a meditation on it.

contemporary.text: The prayer asks the one who repeats it to see one source behind water, light, food and the words of the Veda. Tracing the things one uses every day back to what makes them possible is a way of seeing how much depends on what is rarely noticed. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Pick one thing you used today. How many steps back does it take to reach the sun?
reflect.deeper: The commentator calls the simile ‘like light’ impossible, because the sun is compared only with itself. What does it mean to describe something that has no likeness?
reflect.practice: When you next drink a glass of water, recall the rain and the sun that it came from.

references.text: Sāyaṇa (his anuvāka 15) and Bhāskara (his anuvāka 15) comment on this mantra in a different wording; their comments are cited for what they say of the shared opening and of the mantra’s use. The edition’s computed concordance maps this anuvāka to Sāyaṇa 15 and 28 and to no Bhāskara anuvāka: Sāyaṇa 28 is the alternative breath-control mantra, and Bhāskara 15 is the comment that belongs here.
The last words, āpo jyotī raso ’mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om, are the ‘head’ (śiras) recited with the gāyatrī in breath control (10.35).

flags.note: Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s recensions read this mantra differently after ghṛṇiḥ sūrya ādityaḥ (‘they worship; austerity, truth … that is brahman, that is the waters’); the edition prints the 80-anuvāka text, whose three witnesses agree in substance.
na prabhā is read as a simile with the anonymous commentator; it could be read as a negation.
